analysis.one_liner: Caps credit card interest rates for two years at a formula tied to the prime rate.
analysis.headline: The bill was never acted on by any House committee and died when the 107th Congress ended, with no cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Truth in Lending Act to cap the interest rate on outstanding credit card balances for two years. The cap would equal 5.5% plus the average rate banks charge their best corporate customers (the prime rate, as published in the Wall Street Street Journal), so it would have settled around the low teens — well below what most cardholders pay. After two years the cap would have expired automatically. The bill got a single sponsor, no cosponsors, and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Cardholders who carry a balance from month to month — often households stretching to pay for necessities — would have paid meaningfully less interest while the cap was in effect.

how_it_helps.text: The bill writes a hard ceiling into federal law: for two years, the annual percentage rate on outstanding credit card balances could not exceed 5.5 percentage points above the average prime rate banks charge their best corporate customers. [S3]
Because card rates typically ran well above that formula, cardholders carrying revolving balances would have paid less interest each month for the life of the cap. [S2]
The cap applies automatically across all issuers, so borrowers would not have had to shop around or negotiate to get the lower rate. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers — banks and finance companies — would give up the gap between what they can currently charge and the capped rate. Issuers might respond by tightening credit approvals or raising fees to offset the lost interest income.

drawbacks.text: The cap is temporary: it takes effect 60 days after enactment and expires at the end of two years, so any relief would be short-lived unless Congress extended it. [S3]
A ceiling tied to the prime rate would rise whenever market rates rise, so it would not guarantee any fixed rate for borrowers. [S3]

Lenders have long argued that rate caps on unsecured credit cards ignore the risk of lending to borrowers with weak credit; issuers could respond by denying cards to riskier applicants or shifting costs into fees, which would leave those borrowers worse off. (General policy mechanism, not stated in the bill text.)
The bill only caps rates on outstanding balances; it does nothing about late fees, penalty rates' other charges, or the underlying debt loads that drive card balances. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For two years, the bill would have delivered real savings to millions of households carrying credit card debt at rates well above the cap. The main honest objections are that it is short-lived, it floats with the prime rate rather than setting a fixed ceiling, and issuers might offset lost interest by restricting who can get a card or by charging more fees. On balance, its help for borrowers outweighs those costs, though it would have been a modest, temporary fix rather than lasting reform.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, then to its Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit Subcommittee, and sat there until the 107th Congress ended in January 2003 — no hearing, no vote, ever.

narrative.text: Rep. Max Sandlin introduced the bill on October 12, 2001. [S1]
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services. [S5]
On November 2, 2001, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, the step where it stopped. [S5]
The bill had no cosponsors at any point. [S4]
No version of the bill ever reached the House floor or the Senate; the Congress ended on January 3, 2003, killing the bill. [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers kept the freedom to charge uncapped interest rates, because the bill never advanced past a subcommittee referral. Cardholders carrying balances paid the market rate for another two years and beyond.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit card issuers; cardholders paid market rates

for.name: Rep. Max Sandlin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Credit Card Fairness Act, which would have capped credit card interest rates for two years.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit Subcommittee on November 2, 2001, and never scheduled a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor action, leaving it to die in committee with no cosponsors to force the issue.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors from either party signed on and no votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape of support for the bill cannot be measured from the record.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers (banks and finance companies)
industries.note: The bill would have capped the rate issuers could charge on outstanding balances for two years, cutting interest income in direct proportion to cardholders' savings. Their interest ran against cardholders' in this bill. [S2]
